newsitem.title: USA: Democrats vow to expand health insurance to kids.
newsitem.headline: Democrats vow to expand health insurance to kids.

text.p: Democrats plan an all-out push to expand health coverage to America's 10 million uninsured children, either through a new tax credit or vouchers to families, a top lawmaker said on Thursday.

To address the problem, the Democrats also want to ensure that the Medicaid health programme for the poor, elderly and disabled reaches all eligible children. A recent study found millions of children who qualify do not receive care.
President Bill Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget, to be delivered to Congress next month, was also expected to include initiatives to increase health care for children.
Health Secretary Donna Shalala is said to be pressing a strategy that increases Medicaid outreach to children and also includes other initiatives to expand care.
"Expanding health care to children will be our number-one health priority this year," Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, told a news conference.

"We've conceded we're not going to pass comprehensive health insurance for the forseeable future. But we will never concede that we give up the fight to improve health care ... for families all across the country," he said.
Daschle said providing insurance for children up to age 18 would receive the same attention Democrats gave last session to a bill to help people keep insurance if they change jobs.
But that legislation, signed by Clinton amid great fanfare last year, had bipartisan support from its inception. It was unclear whether Republicans would join the new effort.

Asked about the Democratic plan on Wednesday, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said Democrats apparently were trying "to do with salami slices what they could not do with a bold, government takeover of health care."
Lott said Republicans would have their own health care task force and agenda to provide more choices for Americans.
But Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said on Thursday extending Medicaid to children had proved to be cost-effective in the past.
A top House Republican aide said Republicans were not insensitive to the issue, "obviously we care about kids, too" but wanted to minimise government interference.

Daschle said Democrats would introduce two proposals -- a refundable tax credit to cover insurance costs and a voucher that families could use to buy coverage. If they were successful, Congress would eventually choose one option.

There will be income limits to target aid to families of moderate means, but the Democrats have not decided what range of services to cover or how large the credits or vouchers would be. They would pay for their plan by cutting spending or closing what Daschle called unwarranted tax breaks to corporations.

An insurance plan introduced last session by Massachusetts Democrats Edward Kennedy and John Kerry would have provided a government subsidy on a sliding income scale. Kerry estimated it would cost $24 billion over five years, to be funded by cuts in corporate tax breaks and a tobacco tax increase.

The Employee Benefits Research Institute in October estimated that about 10 million American children, or almost 15 percent, are uninsured. They often end up being treated in the most expensive facilities, such as emergency rooms.

A recent study by the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities found that in 1994 nearly 2.7 million poor children under age 11 who did not have insurance all year and were eligible for Medicaid were not enrolled.
